title: Light a talking head with three household lamps
mechanism_check: Confirm the real problem is light POSITION, not light QUALITY: a dim lamp 2 feet away beats a bright ceiling light 8 feet away. Test by moving your nearest lamp close and watching your face on the phone preview.
Kill the overhead light first: one strong top light creates raccoon eyes that no lamp can fix. The mechanism you want is frontal soft light plus separation from the background.
Check for mixed color temperatures: a warm lamp plus cool window light makes your skin tone fight itself. Pick ONE dominant source and dim or cover the other.
improvised_tools: Two identical lamps for key and fill (desk lamps, floor lamps, even string lights clustered in a jar)
One small lamp or phone flashlight for the hair/back light that separates you from the wall
White shower curtain or bedsheet taped over a lamp to diffuse it instead of a softbox
Books or a chair to raise lamps to face height
steps: Turn OFF all overhead lights and the room's brightest fixture; you want to control the sources, not fight them.
Place your brightest lamp at 45 degrees to one side of your face, 2-3 feet away, at face height. This is your KEY light.
Put the second lamp at 45 degrees on the other side but FARTHER away (4-5 feet). This is FILL — dimmer, so it only softens the key's shadow instead of creating its own.
Place the third small light behind you aimed at the back of your head or the wall behind you. This separates you from the background so you stop blending into it.
Draught the sheet over the key lamp if the light is harsh: softer source = bigger-looking light = better skin. Check the phone preview at each step.
stop_conditions: Stop if a lamp shade or sheet is close enough to a hot bulb to scorch it — LEDs only for improvised diffusion; if you only have hot incandescents, keep fabric 6+ inches away or skip the diffuser.
Stop if the mixed-color problem won't resolve and your skin looks green or gray on preview; re-light with a single source type instead of publishing broken footage.
Stop and simplify to one lamp if adding lights is making the face flatter instead of more dimensional; more light is not better, better-placed light is.

title: Soften harsh light with a bedsheet bounce
mechanism_check: Diagnose first: harsh shadows with hard edges on your face mean a SMALL, hard light source (bare bulb, noon sun). The fix is not less light, it is a BIGGER apparent source — achieved by bouncing it off a large surface.
Check whether the harshness is direction: if the hot side is far brighter than the shadow side, bouncing only fixes it if you return light INTO the shadow side.
Confirm the sheet you plan to use is white or near-white; colored fabric bounces tinted light that looks sickly on skin.
improvised_tools: White flat bedsheet or white shower curtain liner as the bounce/diffusion surface
Clothesline, shower rod, or two chairs with a broom across them to hang the sheet
Tape or binder clips to hold the sheet without sewing
steps: Hang the sheet between the light and your face if the light is glaring (diffusion), or at 45 degrees opposite the key light if you want to fill shadows (bounce).
Move the sheet, not the lamp, to tune: closer sheet to face = softer light; further = stronger but still soft.
Check the phone preview: the shadow edge on your nose and chin should be a soft gradient, not a hard line.
Pin the sheet's corners so it doesn't sag into the shot or blow into the lamp; a pinned sheet is a tool, a draped one is a fire risk.
stop_conditions: Stop if the fabric must sit within 6 inches of a hot (non-LED) bulb to reach you — reposition the lamp instead; scorched fabric is how improvised lights become real fires.
Stop if bouncing kills so much light your phone drops to noisy grain: you bounced too far; move the bounce closer or switch to a stronger source.
Stop using a colored sheet if the cast won't correct in camera — re-shoot with white rather than trusting post to fix a color problem.

title: Record clean dialogue with wired earbuds as a mic
mechanism_check: Diagnose the real enemy: bad audio is almost never the microphone's fault — it is DISTANCE and ROOM. A $3 earbud mic 6 inches from your mouth beats a $300 mic across the room. Fix distance first.
Check the room before recording: clap once and listen for flutter echo (slap-back from bare walls). The mechanism is reflections arriving milliseconds after the direct sound.
Confirm which earbud mic your phone is using: plug the earbuds in fully and tap the mic capsule lightly — you should hear it in a test recording. If not, the phone fell back to its internal mic.
improvised_tools: Wired earbuds (any phone headset with an inline mic) as the boom mic
A sock stretched over the earbud mic as a pop filter and wind screen
Closet full of clothes, or blankets over a door frame, as a deadened recording space
Phone voice-memo app or any free recorder as the capture device (sync to video later with a clap)
steps: Plug in the earbuds, open a recorder, tap the mic capsule, and record 5 seconds to confirm which mic is live.
Clip or tape the earbud mic to your shirt 6 inches below your chin, slightly off-center so breath doesn't hit it directly.
Stretch the sock over the mic capsule and secure it with the clip so it can't shift mid-take.
Record in the deadest corner you have: closet of clothes is ideal. Turn off fans, AC, and fridges — every hum is permanent.
Do a 10-second test take with your loudest and softest delivery, then listen on headphones before shooting the real take.
stop_conditions: Stop if you hear a steady buzz or whine in the test that moves when you move the cable — the earbud cable is picking up interference; reroute it away from power bricks or switch to the phone's internal mic at closer distance.
Stop if the recording peaks and distorts on loud words: back the mic to 8 inches or speak slightly off-axis instead of continuing to record clipped, unfixable audio.
Stop recording outdoors in wind above a light breeze with only a sock screen — it will be garbage; move inside or wait for calm.

title: Frame a solo shot with a phone-stack tripod stand-in
mechanism_check: The mechanism of a bad solo frame is not the missing tripod, it is the CAMERA TOO LOW: a phone on a table looks up your nose. Fix height first, stability second.
Check the rule of thirds with your eyes: your eyes should sit on the upper third line of the frame, headroom small. If there is more wall above your head than face below, the camera is wrong.
Confirm lens cleanliness before building anything: one fingerprint smear defeats any framing work.
improvised_tools: Stack of books, a mug, or a rice-filled sock as a base that holds a phone upright
Rubber bands or a hair tie to lash the phone to the stack so a nudge doesn't topple it
A small mirror or the front camera to check framing while you sit in position
Painter's tape on the floor marking where YOU sit and where the stack goes, so resets are instant
steps: Wipe the lens. Decide your framing: chest-up for talking heads, waist-up for demos.
Stack books to bring the lens to eye level minus 2 inches (slightly below eye level is flattering; far below is not).
Lash the phone to the stack with rubber bands; lean it back 5 degrees so the stack can't drift forward into your shot.
Sit in your tape mark, check the front-camera preview: eyes on the upper third, a little headroom, phone lens between your eyes.
Record 5 seconds, walk over, and verify the frame before the real take — phones crop differently in video mode than in preview.
stop_conditions: Stop if the stack wobbles when you bump the table: rebuild the base wider before shooting, not after the tenth ruined take — unstable framing is a rebuild problem, not a reshoot-till-lucky problem.
Stop if you cannot get the lens to eye level with stable objects in reach; a low angle you hate will not fix itself in post.
Stop shooting if the phone overheats and drops frames in a long take; cool it down and break the shoot into shorter segments instead.

title: Steady handheld footage without a gimbal
mechanism_check: Diagnose the shake: it comes from your STEPS, not your hands. The mechanism is vertical bobbing transmitting through your arms. Everything that works either removes the bob (stance) or decouples it (body as spring).
Check your breathing on the preview: a visible pulse of shake every 2-3 seconds is chest breathing pushing the phone; belly breathing fixes it free.
Confirm what the shot actually needs: locked-off wide, slow push, or walking follow. The technique differs, and guessing wrong is what wastes takes.
improvised_tools: Your own body: elbows tucked to ribs, phone braced against your face/chest (human tripod)
A bag strap, belt, or string looped under the phone and stepped on — a $0 steadicam that tensions out vertical shake
A backpack pressed against a wall, railing, or car door as a field monopod
steps: For locked-off shots: brace both elbows against your ribs, hold the phone against your cheek, exhale fully, and shoot inside that exhale — 10 usable seconds per breath.
For walking shots: bend your knees deep, walk heel-to-toe like a slow duck, and keep the phone at chest height with both hands; the knees eat the bob.
For the string rig: tie a cord to a bolt or clamp on the phone, run it down, and step on it — pull upward gently while shooting; the tension kills vertical jitter.
Shoot everything 20% wider than you want and plan a slight digital stabilize/crop in the edit — stabilization you plan for beats stabilization you hope for.
stop_conditions: Stop walking backward while filming yourself if the ground behind you is unseen — a fall breaks you AND the phone; re-block the shot or get a spotter.
Stop if the take needs to be longer than your exhale-brace can hold: split the shot and cut around it instead of fighting tremor into the footage.
Stop fighting shake in post if the jitter is severe; digital stabilization crops and warps, and warping looks worse than a planned static frame.

title: Run a one-person B-roll capture pass
mechanism_check: Diagnose why solo B-roll fails: it is not lack of crew, it is lack of a SHOT LIST made before the location. The mechanism is decision fatigue — every undecided second on location is a second you are not shooting.
Check the edit's needs first: what does the voiceover mention? Every noun in the script is a B-roll target. No noun left uncovered means no awkward talking-head stretches.
Confirm your main shot already exists (or the script is locked) — B-roll without an edit plan is just a pile of pretty clips you will never place.
improvised_tools: A written shot list: 3 columns — WHAT (the noun), HOW (wide/macro/detail), and DURATION (hold 8+ seconds each)
Your same phone from influencer-004's stack setup, handheld per influencer-005
A gray card or white paper for one white-balance reference frame per location
steps: Lock the script or voiceover first and extract every visual noun into the shot list.

At the location, shoot the list in any order — but shoot each item THREE ways: wide (context), medium (action), macro (texture). The edit will use one; having all three is the professional difference.
Hold every shot a full 8 seconds past when you think you have it — the first 3 seconds are the wobble, the last 5 are the take.
Capture one 10-second room tone and one white-balance frame per location before you leave; you cannot go back for these.
stop_conditions: Stop adding shots not on the list once you have full coverage — B-roll hoarding is procrastination wearing a camera; the edit needs coverage, not volume.
Stop shooting in a location where you don't have permission and someone has asked you to leave; no shot is worth a confrontation that becomes the story.
Stop if light is dying and your footage is going noisy — a deliberate early wrap beats three locations of unusable grain.

title: Read a script hands-free with a laptop as teleprompter
mechanism_check: Diagnose the reading-eyes giveaway: eyes flicking side to side means the text is too FAR from the lens line. The mechanism is angular distance — bring the text within a few degrees of the lens and the flicker disappears.
Check your reading speed honestly: most people read a teleprompter 30% slower than their natural speaking pace. Setting scroll speed to your test pace, not your hope, is the whole fix.
Confirm font size is big enough that you can read it at arm's length without squinting — squinting reads as anger on camera.
improvised_tools: A laptop, tablet, or second phone placed directly beside (or just under) the camera lens
Any free teleprompter app or a word processor in auto-scroll/present mode with large text
Books to raise the laptop screen to lens height
steps: Type or paste the script into large font (36pt+) with double spacing — dense paragraphs make you lose your place.
Set the laptop as close to the lens as physically possible: just under or just beside the phone, screen raised to lens height.
Do a timed read-through at your natural speaking pace and set the scroll speed to match THAT, not faster.
Record with a 5-second silent lead so the first line isn't rushed; pause the scroll at natural breath points.
Watch the playback at 1x: if your eyes visibly track side to side, move the screen closer to the lens and re-shoot.
stop_conditions: Stop if you catch yourself sounding like a newsreader — the script has failed; rewrite it in spoken contractions and short sentences instead of forcing delivery through bad copy.
Stop and memorize the outline instead if the prompter keeps distracting you: three bullet points you OWN beat a script you read.
Stop if eye-tracking is still visible after moving the screen adjacent to the lens; the lens is simply too far from any screen position — go off-script for that shot.

title: Shoot readable night footage with just a phone
mechanism_check: Diagnose first: night footage fails because the phone's auto-exposure picks the BRIGHTEST thing (a streetlamp) and crushes your face to black. The mechanism is exposure metering on the wrong zone — lock exposure on the face and everything follows.
Check what light already exists before adding any: windows, neon signs, store fronts, street lamps. Available light is always your key; you only ADD light where there is none.
Confirm the phone model has a manual/exposure-lock feature in video mode — without it, you are fighting the auto-meter every take.
improvised_tools: Phone flashlight or a second phone's screen (white page at full brightness) as a portable fill
A white shopping bag over a flashlight as a 10-second diffuser
Exposure lock (tap-and-hold on the face in most phone cameras) and manual brightness slider
A dark, matte background choice: shoot against dark walls, not mixed street clutter
steps: Scout the location: stand your subject where an existing light (storefront, window, lamp) hits their face at 45 degrees. This is your free key light.
Tap-and-hold on the face to lock exposure and focus; do not let the meter drift during the take.
If the face is still dark, have a helper (or your off hand) hold a second phone's flashlight 3 feet from the face, slightly above eye line, diffused with the white bag if it is harsh.
Frame TIGHT: medium close-ups at night hide background noise and clutter that wide shots expose.
Shoot a 10-second test and watch it at full brightness before committing to the location.
stop_conditions: Stop if the only available light is directly overhead (parking lots, streetlights) — it makes deep eye sockets that read as sinister; relocate or add frontal fill before shooting.
Stop shooting if the phone is grainy even with exposure locked: the sensor has hit its floor and post will not save it — come back at golden hour instead.
Stop and abandon the location if you are alone in an unsafe area at night with visible gear; no footage is worth your safety.

title: Build a kitchen-table product studio
mechanism_check: Diagnose the amateur look: it is almost never the camera — it is the BACKGROUND. A cluttered kitchen reads clutter; a seamless white field reads 'product.' The mechanism is figure-ground separation, and you can build it from paper.
Check reflections: glossy products double every light source as a glare spot. The fix is diffused, large light sources placed far to the sides — physics, not budget.
Confirm the product's story in one shot: what single action or angle sells it? Build the setup around that, not around the product sitting still.
improvised_tools: White poster board or a roll of kraft paper taped to the table and curved up the wall (a seamless sweep)
Two lamps (influencer-001 rig) with sheet diffusion, placed 45 degrees left and right of the product
Parchment paper as a diffuser for small harsh spots
Phone on the influencer-004 stack, close enough for detail
steps: Tape paper from table edge up the wall behind it, forming a smooth curve with no hard corner — this is your seamless background.
Place the product in the center of the sweep. Set both lamps at 45 degrees to each side, roughly 2 feet away, diffused.
Put the phone on its stack at product level (not looking down at it) and fill the frame.
Shoot the hero angle first: the single image that sells the product. Then rotate 90 degrees for the alternate, then one macro of the key detail.
Check each shot on the phone at full zoom: dust, fingerprints, and price tags show up here, not in the viewfinder of your memory.
stop_conditions: Stop if the product is mirrored/glass and you can see yourself and the room in it — the shoot is reflecting YOUR kitchen; reschedule when you can tent the setup with white sheets or shoot in open shade.
Stop if the client needs shots this setup can't deliver (motion, lifestyle, scale) and be honest about it — a tabletop rig has honest limits.
Stop using paper that is creased or stained mid-shoot: swap the sweep, because the camera sees every flaw you have learned to ignore.

title: Edit a full vertical video start-to-finish on a phone
mechanism_check: Diagnose the edit bottleneck: it is rarely the tool — it is STARTING. The mechanism that finishes edits is a fixed assembly order (structure, then cuts, then captions, then color, then export), never wandering.
Check storage before you begin: a 3-minute project needs roughly 2-4 GB of working space on the phone. An edit that dies at 90% from a full disk is the most common phone-edit failure.
Confirm you have the FINAL audio selected before cutting picture to it — recutting to a new audio track doubles the work.
improvised_tools: Any free mobile editor (CapCut, VN, YouCut, or the platform's own editor) — pick ONE and learn its shortcuts
Cloud or file-app storage for offloading raw clips before you start
Phone auto-captions, then a manual pass fixing names and jargon
steps: Offload everything except the keeper takes to free 4+ GB. Import keepers only.

Assemble in fixed order: (1) lay the audio/voiceover spine, (2) cut picture to it with hard cuts on beats, (3) add captions — auto-generate then fix every error by hand, (4) color: one look applied to all clips (white balance match first), (5) music bed at -20dB under voice, never over.
Export at the platform's native spec (1080x1920, 30fps for most short-form) — wrong aspect ratio is an instant credibility loss.
Watch the export once end-to-end on the phone before posting; the export can glitch in ways the timeline preview hides.
stop_conditions: Stop if the app crashes on export twice — the project file is corrupted or the phone is out of headroom; split the project in half and export the halves instead of losing everything.
Stop adding transitions and effects once the story is clear; every effect past clarity is the edit hiding from being finished.
Stop if auto-captions are wrong on key terms and you are tempted to ship anyway — wrong captions on your own name or product are worse than no captions.

title: Salvage echoey or windy audio without plugins
mechanism_check: Diagnose the damage type: ECHO is repeated room reflections (fix = cut frequencies, shorten decay); WIND is low-frequency rumble under 100 Hz (fix = high-pass); CLIPPING is flattened peaks (unfixable, but you can mask it). Different damage, different repair — identify before touching anything.
Check whether the damage is on the WHOLE track or only in sections: localized damage gets repaired in pieces, not with one global setting that wrecks the good parts.
Confirm you have the original file unedited as a backup — every repair pass should start from the untouched original, never from a previous repair attempt.
improvised_tools: Any free editor with a basic EQ (even phone apps have one): high-pass filter + a notch around 300-500 Hz for room boom
Your ears on headphones — the only meter that matters for repair work
The original unedited file, kept safe and never overwritten
steps: Duplicate the track; all repairs happen on the copy. For wind: apply a high-pass filter at 80-120 Hz — rumble lives below this, voice does not.
For echo/room boom: cut 2-4 dB at 300-500 Hz (the boxy band) and a smaller cut at 2-4 kHz if it sounds harsh. Less is more — repair, don't redesign.
For sections that are truly destroyed, cut them out and cover with B-roll rather than publishing audio that hurts; silence with music under B-roll beats distorted voice.
A/B the repaired section against the original every few moves; ear fatigue lies after 20 minutes, so take breaks.
stop_conditions: Stop if the voice itself is unintelligible under the damage — no EQ restores information that isn't there; re-record the section (ADR with your earbud mic per influencer-003) instead of polishing static.
Stop if repairs are making it sound underwater or robotic: you have cut too much; go back to the original and make HALF the moves.
Stop repairing after 30 minutes on a single clip — diminishing returns have set in; either accept it, re-record, or cut the section.

title: Back up a shoot with no spare drive
mechanism_check: Diagnose the real risk: it is not losing the FILES, it is losing the ONLY copy before a second copy exists anywhere. The mechanism that loses footage is a single point of failure between shoot and home — eliminate that window first.
Check every storage surface you actually have: phone free space, cloud free tiers, a laptop, a friend's phone, a borrowed USB stick. Count them before the shoot ends.
Confirm which clips are irreplaceable (interviews, one-time events) versus re-shootable (B-roll) — triage the backup order by irreplaceability.
improvised_tools: Every free cloud tier you have (drive, photos, dropbox) — even 15 GB holds a day's phone footage
A second phone or laptop as a physical second copy
Your phone's file manager to move (not copy) footage off the camera roll to free shooting space
steps: Before leaving the location: copy irreplaceable clips to the second device or start a cloud upload immediately — the backup window is the drive home, not tonight.
Verify the copy: play 5 seconds of the transferred file on the receiving device. An unverified copy is a rumor, not a backup.
Only after verification, clear the camera roll to free space for the next shoot.
Name the folder with date + project: '2026-09-18-brandshoot'. Future-you finds things by date, not by memory.
stop_conditions: Stop if the cloud upload is stalled on hotel/cafe wifi with hours remaining — pivot to a physical second copy (any device with space) and retry cloud later; a stalled upload is not a backup.
Stop deleting originals to free space before at least one verified copy exists elsewhere — that is the exact sequence that loses shoots.
Stop and buy/borrow storage before the next shoot if you are regularly operating with zero headroom; improvised backup is a bridge, not a system.

title: Build a three-pillar content system from scratch
mechanism_check: Diagnose the randomness problem: creators who post 'whatever feels right' get an incoherent audience. The mechanism is expectation — an audience follows a PREDICTABLE promise, and pillars are three promises you rotate.
Check your own energy, not just market demand: a pillar you cannot sustain for 100 episodes is a trap. Sustainability is a selection criterion, not a footnote.
Confirm the three pillars overlap at your identity: pillar 1 is what you KNOW, pillar 2 is what you LIVE, pillar 3 is what you WONDER about. Together they make a person, not a niche.
improvised_tools: A single page (paper or notes app): three pillar names, each with a one-line promise and 10 seed ideas
Your existing best-performing posts sorted by theme — the data votes on which pillars already work
A weekly calendar slot per pillar (e.g., Mon = pillar 1, Wed = pillar 2, Fri = pillar 3)
steps: Write down everything you could talk about for an hour unprepared. Group them into clusters.
Name the three strongest clusters as pillars, each with a one-line audience promise: 'Pillar 1: X, so you can Y.'
Generate 10 concrete video ideas per pillar (30 total) — this is your idea bank, the thing that ends 'what do I post' mornings.
Assign pillars to weekly slots. Post pillar by pillar in rotation; do not chase a pillar that is 'trending' out of order.
After one month, check which pillar pulls the most saves/shares (not views) and give it the extra slot.
stop_conditions: Stop if a pillar requires research you hate doing — a pillar is a 100-episode commitment; pick a sustainable one instead of a strategic one you will abandon by week 3.
Stop at three pillars: a fourth pillar is just randomness with a label.
Stop if the three pillars have nothing to do with each other — the audience came for a person, and four unrelated strangers in a trench coat is not a person.

title: Build a hook bank of fifty openers
mechanism_check: Diagnose the retention problem honestly: viewers decide in 1-3 seconds whether to stay, and the decision is made on the HOOK, not the content. The mechanism is pattern interruption — the brain stays for what it cannot predict.
Check your own analytics: find your 10 highest-retention videos and transcribe ONLY their first 5 seconds. Your bank should start from what already works on YOUR audience, not a guru's list.
Confirm each hook passes the 'so what' test: if a stranger cannot name why they should care within the sentence, it is a sentence, not a hook.
improvised_tools: A running doc of 50 hooks, categorized: curiosity gap, bold claim, direct callout, story drop, visual shock
Your top-10 retention transcripts as the seed material
A weekly review slot: retire hooks that stop working, promote variants that beat them
steps: Transcribe the first 5 seconds of your 10 best-retention videos; extract the structural pattern of each (question? claim? contradiction?).
Write 5 new hooks per pattern (50 total), each specific to YOUR niche — '3 things' is a pattern, '3 things ruining your sourdough starter' is a hook.
For your next 10 videos, rotate bank hooks deliberately and track retention on each.
Weekly: retire any hook whose retention fell below your average; write 2 variants of each top performer. The bank is alive or it is dead.
stop_conditions: Stop if hooks are getting you views but the comments are 'clickbait' — a hook that out-promises the video burns trust faster than it builds reach; the hook must be a true preview.
Stop writing hooks in the abstract: every hook in the bank must name a specific video it could open, or it is decoration.
Stop if you are on hook 50 and none beat your originals — your bank has become avoidance of the real problem (the content), not a solution to it.

title: Repurpose one long video into twelve platform pieces
mechanism_check: Diagnose the waste: one long video holds 8-15 standalone moments, and each platform rewards a DIFFERENT shape. The mechanism is native formatting — the same idea must be re-cut, re-captioned, and re-framed per platform, not cross-posted raw.

Check the long video for 'clip-ability' BEFORE repurposing: does it contain self-contained 30-60 second segments with their own setup and payoff? If the value only exists in the full arc, repurposing will butcher it.
Confirm per-platform rules: vertical vs square, caption norms, music licensing, and what counts as 'original' (platforms demote watermarked re-uploads from rival apps).
improvised_tools: The long video's transcript (auto-generated, then skimmed) with timestamps marked on every standalone moment
A repurposing map: which moment -> which platform -> which format (clip, carousel, thread, quote card)
The phone editor from influencer-011 for re-framing horizontal footage to vertical (rule of thirds re-crop, not center crop)
steps: Watch the long video at 1.5x and mark every moment that works standalone: a claim, a story, a demo, a reaction. Aim for 8-15 marks.
Assign each mark to its best platform by strength: visual demos -> short-form video; frameworks/lists -> carousels; opinions -> text threads; quotes -> graphics.
Re-cut each piece NATIVE: re-frame to vertical, re-caption from scratch (platform caption culture differs), re-hook the first 2 seconds. Never post the same render everywhere.
Schedule the pieces over 2 weeks, not all at once — one long video should feed a fortnight.
Track which platform's repurposed pieces outperform the original's reach; that is your lead platform.
stop_conditions: Stop if a platform's audience is reacting with 'wrong app for this' — a piece that needs re-shooting for the platform beats a piece that annoys it.
Stop cross-posting with visible watermarks from rival platforms; it gets demoted and looks amateur — export clean from the source project.
Stop repurposing a long video whose core idea flopped: repurposing multiplies REACH, not quality; amplify winners, not losers.

title: Run a weekly cadence with a two-week backlog buffer
mechanism_check: Diagnose the inconsistency trap: creators miss weeks because they produce AND publish in the same week. The mechanism that survives life is the BUFFER — published content is always 2 weeks ahead of production.
Check your real sustainable rate, not your aspirational one: count how many videos you actually finished in the last month and divide by 4. That is your cadence. Aspirational cadences die by week 3.
Confirm what 'done' means: a video is only buffer-eligible when edited, captioned, thumbnailed, and scheduled — a raw clip in the camera roll is not inventory.
improvised_tools: A simple tracker: 3 columns — IDEAS, IN PRODUCTION, BUFFERED (scheduled). Move cards, never keep it in your head
One fixed production block per week (same day, same hours) plus one fixed admin block for scheduling
Scheduled-post features on each platform so buffered content publishes while you sleep
steps: Set your cadence from your real last-month output. Commit to it publicly if accountability helps, privately if it doesn't.
Block one production day: shoot the week's content in ONE session (batching beats daily context-switching).
Edit within 48 hours. A shoot older than a week feels stale to you and gets abandoned — the 48-hour rule is the buffer's immune system.
Schedule each finished piece at least 2 weeks out. The buffer exists so a bad week costs you nothing.
When the buffer drops below 1 week of content, the NEXT production block is an emergency double — protect the buffer like inventory, because it is.
stop_conditions: Stop increasing cadence when the buffer is healthy and growing — more output with a full buffer usually means declining quality, not more growth.
Stop if production blocks are consistently eating rest days: the cadence is set too high for your life; cut the rate before the rate cuts you (see influencer-039).
Stop scheduling further ahead than 3 weeks for trend-sensitive content — a buffer of stale trend pieces is worse than no buffer.

title: Read your analytics and kill what is not working
mechanism_check: Diagnose the vanity-metric blindness: VIEWS measure distribution, not loyalty. The mechanism that predicts growth is RETENTION + SAVES/SHARES — what people finish and pass on. Optimize for the second pair, report the first.

Check the retention GRAPH, not the average: a cliff at 0:03 means the hook failed; a slope at 0:45 means the middle sagged; a cliff at the end means nothing (normal). Different cliffs, different fixes.
Confirm sample size before killing anything: one video is an anecdote, five in a format is data. Kill formats, not videos.
improvised_tools: Platform analytics: retention graphs, traffic sources, and save/share rates per video
A monthly review doc: format name, episodes posted, average retention, saves per view, verdict (scale / fix / kill)
Your hook bank (influencer-016) and pillar map (influencer-015) as the fix-it toolkit
steps: Once a month, pull every video from the last 30 days into the review doc with retention and saves/view.
Mark each format: SCALE (above-average retention AND saves), FIX (one of the two is weak — diagnose which), KILL (both weak across 5+ episodes).
For FIX formats, change ONE variable next month (hook, length, or pacing — never all three) so you know what worked.
For KILL formats: stop them cold. Replace the slot with a SCALE format or a new experiment — dead formats are schedule parasites.
Write the one-line lesson per killed format. A killed format that taught you something is tuition; one that taught nothing is just a loss.
stop_conditions: Stop checking analytics daily — daily numbers are noise that drives reactive decisions; the review is monthly, the work is weekly.
Stop killing a format before 5 episodes: you are measuring your learning curve, not the format's potential.
Stop if 'the data says' is consistently overriding what you actually want to make — an optimized channel you hate running is a failure with good metrics.

title: Build a repeatable series format viewers return for
mechanism_check: Diagnose why one-offs don't compound: a viewer who loves a video has no REASON to return unless the next one is recognizable. The mechanism is the series contract — same container, new contents, every time.
Check your comment section for the contract already forming: 'part 2?', 'do my city next', 'more of these' — the audience tells you which series to build. Listen before inventing.
Confirm the format is producible on your WORST week: if episode 8 needs a crew, a location, and perfect weather, it will die at episode 4.
improvised_tools: A series bible: title, the 3-beat structure, the recurring line/visual, episode length, production checklist
Your pillar map (influencer-015): the series must live inside one pillar, not float
A numbered naming convention ('Rating X Ep.7') so the series is findable and bingeable
steps: Pick the series from audience signals first, your enthusiasm second — the overlap is the sweet spot.
Define the unchanging container: same opening line, same 3 beats, same length, same closing. The contents change; the container never does.
Produce episodes 1-3 before releasing episode 1: the series must survive its own launch week to earn trust.
Release on a fixed day. 'New episode every Tuesday' is a promise; irregular drops are a rumor.
After episode 6, review: does the audience anticipate it (comments before you post)? If yes, protect the slot. If no, the container is wrong — retool, don't just continue.
stop_conditions: Stop if episodes are getting harder to produce, not easier — a series should get CHEAPER with reps; rising effort means the format is wrong for your resources.
Stop the series if you dread making it: a resented series poisons the whole channel. End it with a finale episode, don't ghost it.
Stop adding series: one strong series beats three limping ones. A second series earns its slot only after the first runs itself.

title: Restructure your first three seconds to fix retention
mechanism_check: Diagnose the specific cliff: pull your retention graph and confirm the drop is in seconds 0-3 (hook failure) and not later (pacing failure). Fixing pacing when the hook is broken is surgery on the wrong organ.
Check what the first frame SHOWS, not says: the mechanism is visual promise — a moving, specific, slightly unresolved image holds attention while words alone leak it.
Confirm the video's payoff appears in the first 3 seconds in some form: the brain stays for a promise it has SEEN, not one it was told about.
improvised_tools: Your retention graphs (influencer-019) marking exactly where each video bleeds viewers
A test protocol: same video, two different 3-second opens, posted as separate experiments
Your hook bank (influencer-016) — this entry is its field application
steps: For each underperforming video, identify the single most visual, surprising, or unresolved moment ANYWHERE in the video — even if it is at minute 4.
Re-cut the opening: lead with that moment (the payoff first), then loop back to the setup. Promise-then-deliver beats build-then-reveal on short-form.
Cut all throat-clearing: no 'hey guys,' no logo sting, no 'in today's video.' The first frame is the promise, the first word continues it.
Test the new open against the old on your next similar video: same topic class, different open, compare 3-second retention.
Keep a running list of which open TYPES work for your audience (cold open? question? visual shock?) — that list is your personal retention doctrine.
stop_conditions: Stop if the re-cut open misrepresents the video — a 3-second retention win that raises the later cliff and the 'clickbait' comments is a net loss.
Stop testing opens on videos whose real problem is a sagging middle; you will optimize the doorway while the house is on fire.
Stop if you are re-cutting the same video a third time — ship the lesson into the NEXT video instead of embalming this one.

title: Train on-camera delivery with daily two-minute reps
mechanism_check: Diagnose the stiffness: on-camera awkwardness is not a personality flaw, it is an UNPRACTICED motor skill. The mechanism is reps — the camera is a muscle, and 2 focused minutes daily beats a monthly workshop.
Check your baseline honestly: record 60 seconds of unscripted talk on your niche today and watch it. Note the top 3 tics (filler words, frozen hands, eye-darting). Those are the training targets.
Confirm you are training ONE tic at a time: the brain cannot fix posture, filler words, and pacing in the same rep. Single-variable training is the whole method.
improvised_tools: Phone on the influencer-004 stack, front camera, same spot every day
A 2-minute timer and a one-line daily prompt from your idea bank
A private log: date, tic trained, one honest note on whether it improved
steps: Set up the same shot daily — remove setup friction so the only decision is pressing record.
Pick ONE tic for the week (e.g., filler words). Record 2 minutes on the prompt, speaking as if to one friend.
Watch it back at 1x, counting the tic. Write the count in the log. The number going down IS the training.
Next week, pick the next tic. Old tics get a maintenance check once a month — skills decay without touch-ups.
After 30 days, re-record your baseline prompt and compare. Keep the comparison private; it is fuel, not content.
stop_conditions: Stop if daily reps are becoming dread — drop to 3x/week rather than quitting; consistency at lower volume beats a perfect streak that breaks.
Stop training delivery while ignoring content: a polished presenter with nothing to say is a teleprompter with a pulse.
Stop comparing your day-30 tape to someone's year-5 output; the only valid comparison is your own day-1.

title: Negotiate a brand deal without an agent
mechanism_check: Diagnose the power dynamic: brands negotiate from rate cards, you negotiate from AUDIENCE DATA. The mechanism is asymmetry of information — whoever knows your real numbers (saves, audience demo, past conversion) sets the price.

Check the brand's history: have they worked with creators your size? What did those creators post? A brand that only buys mega-creators will waste your month; a brand with a micro-creator roster is already convinced.

Confirm the deliverable scope BEFORE pricing: one video is not 'one video' — it is concepting, shooting, editing, revisions, usage rights, exclusivity, and timeline. Price the package, never the post.
improvised_tools: A media kit: audience size, demographics, average views, save/share rates, 3 past brand examples with results
Your rate floor: the number below which you walk away, computed from your hours x your rate + usage value
A simple contract checklist: deliverables, revision rounds (cap at 2), usage rights + duration, exclusivity window, payment terms (50% upfront), kill fee
steps: When the brand reaches out, ask for the brief AND their budget range before naming a price — the first number anchors the negotiation; make it theirs.
Price from the checklist: base fee for production + usage multiplier (paid ads usage = 2-3x organic) + exclusivity premium (competitor lockout = +50-100%).
State your rate, then be silent. The pause is the negotiation — whoever speaks first after the number usually concedes.
Get everything in writing before shooting: the checklist as a one-page agreement, signed. Verbal briefs drift; written ones don't.
Deliver, then send a results report (views, saves, link clicks). The report is what turns one deal into a retainer.
stop_conditions: Stop if the brand won't put usage rights or payment terms in writing — handshake deals with brands end in free usage of your face in ads you never approved.
Stop if the exclusivity window exceeds 90 days or covers your whole niche without a premium that justifies it; exclusivity is inventory you are selling.
Stop if the product conflicts with something you have genuinely recommended before — the audience's trust is the asset the brand is renting; spending it on a contradiction bankrupts you.

title: Recover a stalled channel and rebrand without losing the audience
mechanism_check: Diagnose the stall type before touching anything: ALGORITHM stall (reach died but loyal viewers remain) vs AUDIENCE stall (viewers left because the content drifted) vs CREATOR stall (you burned out and it shows). The fix differs completely; most rebrands fail because they treat an audience stall like an algorithm stall.

Check the data: compare your last 20 videos' retention to the channel's historical average. If retention held while reach died, the audience is still yours — don't rebrand, re-distribute. If retention died first, the content broke before the algorithm did.
Confirm what the remaining core audience actually wants: poll them, read 100 comments, and find the overlap between what they ask for and what you can sustain.
improvised_tools: Your analytics export (influencer-019 review) with retention trends, not just views
A direct audience poll: 3 options for the channel's next direction, voted by the people who still watch
A 90-day transition plan, not a relaunch event — relaunches spike and die; transitions compound
steps: Announce nothing dramatic. Shift the content mix gradually: 80% old / 20% new for a month, then 50/50, then 20/80. The audience follows a bridge, not a cliff.
Keep the series and formats that still retain (influencer-020) running through the whole transition — they are the load-bearing walls.
Address the change once, honestly, in your own voice: what is changing, what is staying, why. One video, no apology tour.
Update branding (name, visuals, bio) only AFTER the content mix has already shifted — branding follows content, never leads it.
At day 90, compare retention and saves/view against the stall baseline. If both recovered, the rebrand worked. If not, the problem was never the brand.
stop_conditions: Stop if the 'rebrand' is really you avoiding the fact that you stopped enjoying the niche — no rebrand fixes creator stall; rest or a genuine pivot does (see influencer-039).
Stop changing the name/visuals more than once in the transition; repeated rebrands read as instability and each one resets recognition.

Stop if the core audience is actively hostile to the new direction in comments AND retention — you are not rebranding, you are starting over; be honest about it and launch clean instead of dragging a resentful audience.

title: Turn comments and DMs into your next content calendar
mechanism_check: Diagnose the idea drought honestly: it is not a creativity shortage, it is a LISTENING shortage. The mechanism is demand capture — your audience is literally writing your content briefs in the comments; the skill is harvesting them systematically.
Check the comment patterns, not individual comments: three people asking the same question is a video; one person asking is a reply. Volume is the signal.
Confirm you are harvesting QUESTIONS and OBJECTIONS, not praise — praise feels good and teaches nothing; objections are content with the tension pre-installed.
improvised_tools: A weekly 20-minute harvest ritual: newest comments + DMs, copied into a doc, tagged by theme
Your idea bank (influencer-015): harvested items go straight in as titled video concepts, not vague notes
A reply-first habit: answer the question in a comment within 24h, then expand the best ones into full videos
steps: Weekly, read every comment and DM from the last 7 days. Copy each question, objection, and 'can you cover X' into the harvest doc.
Tag by theme. Any theme with 3+ hits becomes a titled video concept in the idea bank, credited to the askers ('You asked: ...').
Reply to the original askers when the video drops — tag them. This closes the loop and trains the audience to keep feeding you ideas.
Track which harvested videos outperform your average: that ratio is your proof that listening beats guessing.
stop_conditions: Stop if harvesting is replacing your own ideas entirely — an audience-fed channel drifts toward the lowest common denominator; keep at least a third of the calendar from your own pillar vision.
Stop engaging with bad-faith comments as 'content opportunities' — outrage bait harvests an audience you don't want.
Stop if DMs are becoming a support desk you can't staff; set a boundary (weekly Q&A video instead of 1:1 replies) before resentment sets in.

title: Design a thumbnail and title system that converts
mechanism_check: Diagnose the click problem: click-through is decided by the thumbnail/title PAIR as one unit, not either alone. The mechanism is curiosity with a promise — the image shows the WHAT, the title withholds the WHY (or vice versa), and the brain clicks to close the gap.
Check your own click-through data per video: below your channel average means the packaging failed, regardless of content quality. Packaging is a separate skill from content — judge it separately.
Confirm the promise is TRUE before optimizing: a converting package on a disappointing video trains the audience not to click next time. Conversion compounds only on delivered promises.
improvised_tools: A packaging template: 3 thumbnail layouts (face+object, before/after, text-tease) and 5 title formulas from your hook bank
Your click-through rate per video, reviewed monthly alongside influencer-019
A 'swipe file' of 20 high-performing packages in YOUR niche — study the pattern, never copy the design
steps: For each video, write 3 title options from your hook bank formulas and sketch 2 thumbnail concepts BEFORE editing — packaging decisions made during editing get rushed.
Build the thumbnail at small size first: if it doesn't read at stamp-size on your phone, it won't read in the feed. Big face or object, 3 words max, high contrast.
Pair deliberately: thumbnail shows, title tells — never both saying the same thing. 'I tried X for 30 days' + a shocked face holding the result beats either alone.
After posting, log the click-through rate next to the package type. Monthly, keep the top 2 layouts and retire the bottom one.
A/B test when the platform allows: same video, two packages, 48 hours each. One variable at a time.
stop_conditions: Stop if packaging is outperforming content (high CTR, low retention) — you have a clickbait pipeline; fix the video (influencer-021), not the thumbnail.
Stop using a swipe-file design verbatim from a bigger creator — the audience recognizes the theft and it reads as derivative, not professional.
Stop if you are spending more time on the thumbnail than the video; packaging is the door, not the house.

title: Combine every platform into one cross-posting pipeline
mechanism_check: Diagnose the fragmentation tax: every platform you post to manually costs context-switching, and manual cross-posting is where quality dies (wrong aspect ratios, stale captions). The mechanism that scales is a SINGLE source project feeding platform-native renders — one edit, many outputs.
Check which platform is your LEAD (where growth actually happens) versus SUPPORT (where presence matters): the pipeline serves the lead first and adapts for support, never the reverse.

Confirm the legal/licensing layer: music licensed on one platform may be flagged on another; branded-content disclosures differ per platform. The pipeline must carry compliance per output, not assume one disclosure fits all.
improvised_tools: A master project file per video (the long-form or the full-res vertical master) that all renders derive from
A platform spec sheet: aspect ratio, max length, caption norms, music rules, disclosure requirements per platform
A scheduling tool or calendar that holds the staggered release order (lead platform first, support follows over days)
steps: Produce the master first: full-quality, full-length, clean exports with no platform watermarks.
Render platform-native versions from the master per the spec sheet: re-frame, re-caption, re-hook (influencer-017's method, systematized).
Release in stagger order: lead platform day 1, secondary day 2-3, long-tail (search-driven platforms) day 5+. Each post links or funnels toward the lead where sensible.
Carry compliance per render: disclosures, music swaps, and rights notes checked against the spec sheet before each publish — this is a checklist step, not a memory step.
Monthly, review per-platform growth against effort: a platform eating 20% of pipeline time for 2% of growth gets demoted to presence-only (repost, no native work).
stop_conditions: Stop if a platform's algorithm starts punishing cross-posted content (demotion of non-original): that platform exits the pipeline and gets native-only content or nothing.
Stop adding platforms to the pipeline past the point where quality holds — a pipeline feeding 6 platforms badly is worse than 2 platforms well.
Stop if compliance is being skipped 'to save time' — one undisclosed ad or unlicensed track can cost the whole channel; the checklist is non-negotiable.

title: Protect the voice: personal refinement routines for creators
mechanism_check: Diagnose the real asset: your VOICE — literally (vocal cords) and figuratively (perspective). The mechanism of creator longevity is asset maintenance: vocal rest, sleep, and input diet determine output quality more than any tactic.
Check the input-output balance: if everything you consume is in your niche, your output will be derivative. The mechanism is cross-pollination — originality comes from OUTSIDE inputs recombined.
Confirm the burnout early signals honestly: dreading the camera, resenting comments, fantasizing about quitting. These are maintenance alerts, not character flaws.
improvised_tools: A vocal hygiene baseline: water during recording, no shouting takes back-to-back, 10 minutes of silence after long sessions
A sleep floor: the non-negotiable hours below which you do not shoot (tired delivery reads as bored delivery)
An input diet: for every hour of niche content consumed, one hour of something unrelated (books, walks, other crafts)
A weekly offline block: one half-day with no posting, no analytics, no DMs — the nervous system needs a Sabbath
steps: Set the sleep floor and the weekly offline block first — these are the foundation; tactics sit on top.

Before recording days: hydrate, warm up the voice with 2 minutes of humming/lip trills, and do one non-screen activity first (walk, stretch) so you arrive at the camera as a person, not a content machine.
Curate inputs deliberately: follow 5 creators OUTSIDE your niche for every 5 inside it. Your next original idea is hiding in another field.
Monthly, ask the burnout questions in writing: am I dreading the camera? resenting the audience? If yes to either two months running, run influencer-039's protocol — don't wait for collapse.
stop_conditions: Stop shooting when you are sick with anything affecting the voice — strained vocal takes are unusable anyway, and pushing through can cause real damage; rest is the professional move.
Stop if 'protecting the voice' becomes avoiding all discomfort: growth lives at the edge of the comfort zone; the routines protect the asset, they don't shrink the ambition.

Stop and get real help (not a course entry) if burnout signals persist past a month of rest — persistent dread, sleep disruption, or hopelessness are health matters, and this entry is maintenance, not treatment.

title: Aim content at one named audience persona
mechanism_check: Diagnose the vague-content problem: 'content for everyone' is content for no one. The mechanism is specificity — a named person with a named problem forces concrete choices about topic, tone, and depth that 'the audience' never will.
Check that the persona is REAL, not aspirational: base them on an actual follower, commenter, or past version of yourself. Invented personas produce invented content.
Confirm the persona has a problem you can solve repeatedly: a persona without a recurring pain is a character sketch, not a targeting tool.
improvised_tools: One persona card: name, age/context, their #1 recurring problem, what they've already tried, what a win looks like for them
Three real comments or DMs that this persona could have written — the evidence they're real
Your pillar map (influencer-015): the persona must want what at least one pillar promises
steps: Write the persona card from a real person: name them, describe their situation in 5 lines, and state their recurring problem in their own words.
Tape the card where you see it while scripting. For every video idea, ask: 'Would [Name] click this? Would it solve their problem?' If no, the idea waits.
Script one video directly TO them — use their name in your head, answer their specific objection. Notice how much sharper the content gets.
After a month, check: did persona-targeted videos retain better? If yes, the persona is accurate. If no, the persona is wrong — rewrite the card, don't abandon the method.
stop_conditions: Stop if the persona is so narrow you can't find 50 video ideas for them — the persona needs a recurring problem, not a one-time question.
Stop letting the persona veto everything you personally want to make; they are a targeting tool, not a warden. Keep a personal-joy slot in the calendar.
Stop if you're writing for a persona you no longer respect or relate to — outgrowing your audience happens; that's a rebrand conversation (influencer-024), not a persona tweak.

title: Price your rates and defend them with data
mechanism_check: Diagnose the underpricing cycle: creators price from follower count because it's visible, but brands BUY outcomes. The mechanism is value-based pricing — your rate should track the business result (reach x engagement x conversion history), not the vanity number.
Check your real numbers: cost per engaged view (total fee / (views x engagement rate)) from past deals. This single number lets you compare any offer to your history instantly.
Confirm your floor includes ALL costs: production hours, revision rounds, usage licensing, exclusivity, and the opportunity cost of the organic content the sponsored slot displaces.
improvised_tools: A rate card with three tiers: organic mention, dedicated video, full campaign (video + shorts + usage rights) — each with a floor you will not go below
Your past-deal ledger: brand, fee, deliverables, views, engagement, any conversion data — the evidence that defends the rate
The influencer-023 negotiation checklist as the deal-closing companion to this pricing entry
steps: Compute your floor per tier: (hours x your hourly rate) + usage value + exclusivity premium. Write it down. This number is private and non-negotiable.
Set public rates 30-50% above the floor — the gap is negotiation room, and brands expect to negotiate.

When a brand lowballs, counter with data, not emotion: 'My last 3 dedicated videos averaged X engaged views; at your offer that's $Y per thousand engaged — my floor is $Z.' Numbers end haggling; feelings extend it.
Raise rates every 2-3 deals or every 6 months, whichever comes first. Announce nothing; just quote the new number.
Track every deal in the ledger. After 10 deals you have a market dataset no agent can argue with.
stop_conditions: Stop discounting for 'exposure' from brands with real marketing budgets — exposure doesn't pay rent, and a brand that can't pay isn't a partner, it's a risk.
Stop if you're saying yes to everything at your floor: a full calendar at floor rates means your rates are too low — raise them until ~30% of inquiries walk away.
Stop working with brands that consistently pay late even at good rates; cash-flow damage compounds, and late payers reveal how they'll treat every other term.

title: Run a two-person shoot: shooter plus talent
mechanism_check: Diagnose the coordination failure: two-person shoots fail when BOTH people try to do BOTH jobs. The mechanism is role lock — one brain owns the frame, one brain owns the performance, and neither crosses the line mid-take.
Check the power dynamic before the shoot: if the talent is also the boss, the shooter won't call 'cut' on a bad take. Name explicitly who can stop a take and for what reasons.
Confirm the shot list is shared and agreed BEFORE anyone picks up a camera — on-set negotiation about what to shoot is how two-person shoots burn daylight.
improvised_tools: A shared shot list (influencer-006's format) that both people have seen
Role cards for the day: SHOOTER (owns framing, focus, audio check, calls cut for technical) and TALENT (owns delivery, energy, calls cut for performance)
A 2-minute pre-shoot huddle ritual: shot list review, who-calls-cut agreement, and the day's one priority ('today we get the interview clean; B-roll is bonus')
steps: Huddle: review the shot list, lock roles, agree on cut authority, state the day's one priority.
Shooter sets the frame and audio while talent warms up separately — parallel work, not sequential.

During takes, the shooter watches ONLY technical (framing drift, audio levels, focus); the talent thinks ONLY about delivery. If the shooter sees a technical fault, they call cut immediately — a bad take caught early saves a reshoot.
After each setup, both review the take together on the phone: talent checks performance, shooter checks technical. Two yeses or re-shoot.
Wrap with a 2-minute debrief: what worked, what to change next time. Log it.
stop_conditions: Stop if roles are collapsing (shooter directing performance AND talent framing shots) — call a 5-minute reset and re-lock roles; blurred roles produce takes nobody owns.
Stop the shoot if either person is too tired to do their role well — a tired shooter misses focus, a tired talent phones it in; pushing through wastes both people's day.
Stop if the talent won't accept technical cuts ('just fix it in post') — say plainly that unfixable takes are being recorded, and let them choose: re-shoot now or accept the flaw.

title: Coordinate a multi-creator collab shoot day
mechanism_check: Diagnose the collab chaos pattern: multi-creator shoots fail on LOGISTICS, not creativity — who brings what, who shoots when, who posts what and when. The mechanism is a shared run-of-show: one doc that answers every 'wait, what are we doing' question before it's asked.
Check incentives honestly: each creator needs a clear win (content, audience crossover, or pay). Unnamed incentives breed resentment by hour 4 — name them in the planning doc.
Confirm posting rights and tagging agreements BEFORE shooting: who posts what, when, and who gets tagged. Post-shoot arguments about 'my clip' are the #1 collab killer.
improvised_tools: A run-of-show doc: timeline, locations, who's in which segment, gear assignments, posting schedule with tags
A group chat created at planning time (not shoot day) for logistics only
A simple collab agreement: posting windows (e.g., all post within 48h), tagging, and who owns raw footage
One coordinator (not the most-followed creator — the most organized person) with final say on schedule
steps: Two weeks out: coordinator drafts the run-of-show; every creator confirms their segments, gear, and incentives in writing.
One week out: lock the posting plan — order, timing, tags, and cross-promotion commitments. No 'we'll figure it out on the day.'
Shoot day: coordinator runs the clock, not the camera. Segments run back-to-back per the doc; overruns get cut, not extended — the doc is the boss.
Each creator leaves with their raw footage same-day (transfer before anyone goes home). Footage held hostage kills future collabs.
Posting window: everyone posts per the plan within 48 hours and engages on each other's posts in the first hour — the algorithm rewards the coordinated spike.
stop_conditions: Stop if a creator wants to renegotiate posting rights or revenue split ON the shoot day — pause their segments until it's resolved; shooting under disputed terms produces content nobody can publish.
Stop the day if the schedule has slipped 2+ hours with no recovery path — cut remaining segments by priority rather than grinding everyone into a resentful 12-hour day.
Stop inviting a creator back (quietly, after) if they missed their posting window without communication — reliability is the collab currency; one no-show spends it all.

title: Improvise a crew from volunteers at a live event
mechanism_check: Diagnose the volunteer problem: untrained helpers fail at JUDGMENT calls (when to cut, what to frame), not at mechanical tasks. The mechanism is task design — give volunteers mechanical, single-decision jobs and keep all judgment with yourself.
Check each volunteer's actual capability in 60 seconds: hand them the phone, ask them to hold a frame on you for 10 seconds. Steady hands and listening ears are the only qualifications that matter.
Confirm the event's permission landscape: some venues forbid tripods, flash, or filming certain areas. A volunteer getting confronted by security is YOUR failure to brief them.
improvised_tools: A 2-minute briefing script per role: what to do, what NOT to do, and the one signal that means 'stop and find me'
Role badges or simple labels: CAMERA (hold this frame), AUDIO (hold this mic near speakers), RUNNER (batteries, water, crowd wrangling)
Your phone on a stack (influencer-004) as the locked-off master shot that survives even if every volunteer fails
Spare batteries and storage — volunteers can't improvise power
steps: Before the event: set your locked-off master shot first. This is the guaranteed footage; everything volunteers capture is bonus.
Brief each volunteer with the script: demonstrate the exact frame or mic position, show them the stop signal, tell them what NOT to touch.
Assign ONE mechanical job per person. Never give a volunteer two jobs — divided attention is how both fail.
Check in at natural breaks: swap batteries, review one clip per volunteer (praise the good, correct the framing drift), re-brief as needed.
After: thank them by name in the credits or post, and send them their favorite clip. Volunteers who feel seen come back.
stop_conditions: Stop if a volunteer is filming people who have asked not to be filmed — pull them immediately; consent violations are your liability, not theirs.
Stop relying on volunteers for the critical shot: if the master locked-off camera dies, YOU fix it — never send a volunteer to troubleshoot your core gear mid-event.
Stop the event coverage (not the event) if security or organizers object — argue never; comply, note what was lost, and cover the rest from the audience's perspective.

title: Hand off an edit to a teammate without losing your style
mechanism_check: Diagnose the handoff failure: editors don't ruin style from incompetence — they ruin it from GUESSING. The mechanism is a style spec: every 'I just know it when I see it' preference must become a written rule before handoff.

Check whether YOUR style is actually consistent first: pull 5 of your videos and list what they share (cut pace, caption style, color, music bed level). If you can't list it, the editor can't replicate it — write the spec from the evidence.

Confirm the feedback loop format before the first handoff: timestamped notes on the export, one revision round per pass, and a rule that 'make it pop' is a banned phrase — vague notes produce random edits.
improvised_tools: A one-page style spec: cut pace (e.g., cut on beats, no shot over 4s), caption font/size/position, color look reference, music bed level (-20dB), 3 'never do this' rules
A reference export: one of your best videos as the 'edit like this' north star
A shared project template with your caption presets, color LUT, and export settings pre-loaded
A feedback format: timestamps + specific change + reason ('0:42 — cut 2s, the pause kills pacing')
steps: Write the style spec from your own 5-video audit. Include the 3 nevers — they're the fastest way to communicate taste.
Give the editor the template, the spec, and the reference export. Assign a SMALL first project (one short), not the flagship video.
Review the first export with timestamped notes only. Mark what matched the spec (reinforce) and what didn't (correct with the rule, not taste).
Two clean handoffs in a row = trust earned: graduate to bigger projects. One messy handoff = spec gap: update the spec with the new rule you discovered.
Quarterly, re-audit: pull the editor's recent work next to yours. Drift is normal; the spec gets a maintenance pass.
stop_conditions: Stop if you're rewriting every edit the teammate makes — the handoff has failed; either the spec is incomplete (fix it) or the fit is wrong (admit it). Silent re-editing trains nothing.
Stop adding new style rules mid-project; new rules apply to the NEXT project. Moving the target mid-edit destroys trust.
Stop the handoff entirely if the editor ships your content with errors you have to catch every time (wrong names, bad captions) — reliability is the floor; style is the ceiling.

title: Run a fifteen-minute weekly team content standup
mechanism_check: Diagnose the meeting bloat: content teams drown in status meetings because nobody separates DECISIONS from UPDATES. The mechanism is the 15-minute box: updates are written beforehand, the meeting is only for blockers and decisions.
Check that everyone actually needs to be there: if someone has no blockers and no decisions needed two weeks running, they go async. Meetings are a tax; levy it only where it buys something.
Confirm the standup has a single owner who starts on time and ends on time — a standup without a timekeeper becomes a hangout, and hangouts don't ship content.
improvised_tools: A shared async update doc filled BEFORE the meeting: each person — shipped last week, shipping this week, one blocker (or 'none')
A 15-minute timer, visible to all
A decision log: date, decision, owner, deadline — one line each
A parking lot list for anything that needs more than 2 minutes (it leaves the standup)
steps: Everyone fills the async doc 1 hour before. No doc, no voice in the meeting — the rule enforces itself.
Round-robin, 2 minutes each: blocker first, then the one decision needed. Updates are already read; don't re-read them aloud.
Anything needing discussion goes to the parking lot with an owner and a separate 20-minute slot — the standup never runs over.
End with the decision log read-back: each decision, its owner, its deadline. Ambiguity dies here.
Post the log in the team channel. Next week's standup opens by checking last week's deadlines.
stop_conditions: Stop if the standup regularly runs over 20 minutes — the parking lot discipline has failed; the owner must get stricter or the meeting loses its authority.
Stop inviting people with no blockers and no decisions for the third week running — move them async; a meeting they don't need is morale damage.
Stop if decisions logged aren't being executed by next week — the standup is theater; fix accountability (who owns what, what happens on a miss) before holding another one.

title: Teach a teammate to shoot in your style in one session
mechanism_check: Diagnose the teaching failure: people teach style by TALKING about it ('make it cinematic'), but style is a set of DECISIONS. The mechanism is decision transfer — the trainee must make your decisions with you correcting in real time, not hear your philosophy.
Check the trainee's baseline first: have them shoot 60 seconds their way before you teach anything. You need to see their defaults to know what to overwrite.
Confirm one session means ONE skill layer: framing this week, lighting next week. Teaching the whole style in 2 hours produces a trainee who remembers none of it.
improvised_tools: Your style spec (influencer-034) condensed to a 5-rule field card they can hold
A practice subject and location with zero stakes (not a client shoot, not a deadline)
Their baseline 60-second clip from before the session, for the before/after comparison
steps: Show the baseline clip back to them with 3 specific notes tied to the field card rules — evidence first, instruction second.
Demonstrate ONE rule live: set the shot, narrate each decision ('lens at eye level because...'), then hand them the camera.
They shoot the same setup while you watch silently. Correct only violations of the 5 rules — let small imperfections live; you're installing the framework, not the finish.
Repeat with 3 different setups. By the third, they should be narrating the decisions themselves — that's the transfer moment.
End with the before/after comparison and assign one rule to practice solo this week. Next session covers the next layer.
stop_conditions: Stop if you're re-shooting their practice takes yourself to 'show them' — you've become the shooter again and they're watching; hand the camera back.
Stop the session if frustration is rising on either side — a 10-minute break beats an hour of tense reps; motor skills don't install under stress.
Stop teaching new layers if the current layer isn't sticking after 3 sessions — the trainee may need a different role on the team, and that's a staffing insight, not a failure.

title: Share gear between collaborators without losing or breaking it
mechanism_check: Diagnose the gear-loss pattern: shared gear doesn't get lost from malice — it gets lost from AMBIGUITY about who has what. The mechanism is a checkout log: every item has a named holder at all times, or it doesn't exist.

Check the gear's real value before lending: replacement cost, not purchase price. If losing it would hurt, it gets the full protocol; if it's a $10 cable, it gets the light version. Match process to stakes.
Confirm the borrower's transport plan: most gear damage happens in transit, not in use. 'How are you getting it home' is a lending question, not small talk.
improvised_tools: A shared checkout log: item, holder, date out, date due, condition photo at handoff
Condition photos taken at every handoff (30 seconds, kills 100% of 'it was already like that')
A communal 'consumables' kit (batteries, cables, gaffer tape, SD cards) that doesn't need checkout — only the expensive items do
Padded bags or cases for anything that leaves the building
steps: Log every lend: photo the item's condition, note the holder and due date in the shared log. Both parties see it — no private loans of shared gear.
Borrower confirms the transport plan out loud: case, vehicle, no checked luggage for cameras. If the plan is bad, the loan doesn't happen.
On return: photo again, compare, log it back. Damage found at return gets discussed immediately, not discovered weeks later.
Monthly: audit the log. Anything overdue 2+ weeks gets a direct ask. The log only works if it's enforced.
stop_conditions: Stop lending an item to someone who returned the last loan damaged without discussion — pattern borrowers don't get third chances on expensive gear.
Stop if the checkout log isn't being used — an unenforced log is worse than no log (false confidence); either recommit the team to it or stop sharing the expensive items.

Stop and replace (not repair-by-hope) any safety-critical item that's damaged: frayed power cables, cracked tripod heads under load. Gear failure mid-shoot is a safety issue, not just an inconvenience.

title: De-escalate conflict on a shoot day before it kills the session
mechanism_check: Diagnose the conflict type fast: LOGISTICS conflict (schedule, roles — solvable with the doc), CREATIVE conflict (vision differences — solvable with a test), and EGO conflict (status, credit — not solvable on set, only contained). Treating ego conflict like logistics conflict pours fuel on it.

Check your own state first: if YOU are the escalated one, you cannot de-escalate anyone. The mechanism is co-regulation — the calmest nervous system in the room sets the ceiling. Step away for 60 seconds if needed.
Confirm what's actually at stake: most shoot-day fights are about 5% of the day's output. Name the real stakes out loud — it shrinks most conflicts instantly.
improvised_tools: A pre-agreed pause signal anyone can call (hand up, 'reset') that stops the shoot for 5 minutes, no questions asked
The run-of-show or shot list as the neutral arbiter — 'the doc says' defuses better than 'I say'
A private channel: pull the person aside, never litigate in front of the group — audiences make people defend positions they'd otherwise drop
Separate the people from the problem out loud: 'we both want the segment to work; we disagree on the angle'
steps: Call the pause at the first sign of heat — raised voices, sarcasm, stonewalling. Early pauses cost 5 minutes; late ones cost the day.
Separate: take the heated person aside privately. Listen for 2 minutes without rebuttal — most people de-escalate once they feel heard.
Name the conflict type out loud: 'This sounds like a logistics clash — the doc says X, you need Y. Let's adjust the doc.' Type-naming gives everyone a ladder down.
Resolve to a test when it's creative: 'We shoot it your way once, my way once, decide at the edit.' Tests end arguments; opinions extend them.
Log what happened after wrap — not to punish, to pattern-match. Three conflicts with the same person is a collaboration-fit signal.
stop_conditions: Stop the shoot for the day if anyone is shouting, threatening, or refusing to continue — a finished shoot isn't worth a broken working relationship or anyone's safety; wrap, cool off, regroup tomorrow.
Stop trying to mediate if YOU are a party to the conflict — bring in the neutral coordinator or postpone the decision; biased mediation breeds resentment.

Stop collaborating with someone after repeated ego conflicts (3+) even if the content is good — the content is never worth a team that dreads shoot days. This is a safety stop for the team's longevity.

title: Stop the grind: a burnout protocol for creator teams
mechanism_check: Diagnose the burnout stage honestly: STRAIN (tired but recovering on rest days), BURNOUT (rest doesn't fix it, dread is constant), BREAKDOWN (physical symptoms, can't function). The mechanism differs per stage — strain needs rest, burnout needs structural change, breakdown needs professional help. Mis-staging the response wastes the intervention.
Check the team's load data, not vibes: hours worked, buffer depth (influencer-018), missed rest days, revision rounds per video. Burnout leaves a paper trail before it leaves a body count.

Confirm psychological safety first: if admitting exhaustion is punished (overtly or subtly), no protocol works. The team lead goes first — 'I'm at strain stage' said by the lead unlocks honesty for everyone.
improvised_tools: A monthly 5-question pulse check, anonymous: energy level, dread level, rest days taken, workload fairness, one thing to change
Pre-agreed load-shedding rules: when the buffer drops below 1 week, cadence drops automatically (no meeting, no guilt) — the rule decides, not a debate
A rest-day floor: minimum days off per month, tracked like deliverables
The buffer system (influencer-018) as the structural shock absorber — burnout protocol without a buffer is just advice
steps: Monthly, run the pulse check. Anyone at burnout stage triggers the protocol — no debate, no 'push through this launch.'
Immediate: cut their load 50% for 2 weeks via the load-shedding rules. The buffer covers the gap — that's what it's for.
Structural: identify what broke them (revision churn? always-on DMs? no rest days?) and fix the SYSTEM, not the person. A rested person returning to the same grinder re-burns in a month.
Re-entry: graduated return, not a cliff — half load week 1, three-quarter week 2, full week 3, with a check-in at each step.
Quarterly, the lead reviews the team's aggregate pulse data and reports what changed. A protocol nobody audits is a poster.
stop_conditions: Stop and get professional help (not a team protocol) if anyone shows breakdown-stage signs: persistent hopelessness, physical symptoms, inability to function — this entry is a team process, not treatment, and saying so is the responsible move.
Stop the protocol from becoming surveillance: pulse data is for load decisions, never for performance reviews. One misuse destroys trust permanently.
Stop normalizing 60+ hour weeks as 'hustle' in team culture — if the protocol keeps triggering, the business model is the problem, not the people. Fix the model or shrink the team honestly.

title: Write the team's style bible together
mechanism_check: Diagnose why style bibles fail: they're usually written by ONE person and resented by everyone else. The mechanism is co-authorship — a bible the team writes together gets followed; a bible handed down gets quietly ignored.

Check that the team actually HAS a shared style first: pull everyone's recent work and find the common threads. If there's no commonality, you're writing aspirations, not documenting — that's fine, but label it honestly as 'target style v1.'
Confirm the bible's scope: it covers repeatable craft decisions (framing, pacing, captions, color, tone), NOT creative vision per video. A bible that tries to legislate creativity becomes a cage.
improvised_tools: A shared doc with sections: visual (framing, lighting, color), edit (pace, captions, music), voice (tone, phrases, nevers), workflow (file naming, handoff, export specs)
5 reference videos the team agrees represent the style — the evidence the rules describe
A quarterly review slot: the bible is versioned (v1.0, v1.1), never finished
steps: In a 90-minute workshop, the team watches the 5 reference videos together and names what they share — each shared trait becomes a rule, written in plain language with an example.
Draft the four sections live in the doc. Every rule needs a WHY (the reason it exists) — rules without reasons get broken first.
Each member 'owns' one section as its maintainer — ownership distributes the upkeep and the pride.
Test-drive for 2 weeks: every new video gets checked against the bible; gaps and bad rules surface fast.
Lock v1.0 after the test drive. Quarterly review: what's outdated, what's missing, what did we outgrow. Version it.
stop_conditions: Stop if one person is dictating the whole bible while others stay silent — that's not co-authorship; pause and run the workshop as anonymous contributions first, then discuss.
Stop adding rules past the point of usability: a 40-page bible nobody opens is worse than a 2-page one everyone follows. If it doesn't fit on one screen per section, cut.
Stop treating the bible as permanent law — a style that can't evolve is a style that dies; the quarterly review is mandatory, not optional.
